In [[physics]], the '''Weyl expansion''', also known as the '''Weyl identity''' or '''angular spectrum expansion''', expresses an outgoing [[spherical wave]] as a [[linear combination]] of [[plane wave]]s. In a [[Cartesian coordinate system]], it can be denoted as{{sfn|Chew|1990|p=65-75}}{{sfn|Kinayman|Aksun|2005|p=243-244}}
{{short description|Outgoing spherical wave as a linear combination of plane waves}}
:<math>\frac{e^{-i k_0 r}}{r}=\frac{1}{ 2\pi i} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} dk_x dk_y e^{-i(k_x x + k_y y)} \frac{e^{-ik_z |z|}}{k_z}</math>,

where <math>k_x</math>, <math>k_y</math> and <math>k_z</math> are the [[wavenumber]]s in their respective coordinate axes:

:<math>k_0=\sqrt{k_x^2+k_y^2+k_z^2}</math>.

The expansion is named after [[Hermann Weyl]], who published it in 1919.<ref name="weyl-original"/> The Weyl identity is largely used to characterize the reflection and transmission of spherical waves at planar interfaces; it is often used to derive the [[Green's function]]s for [[Helmholtz equation]] in layered media. The expansion also covers [[evanescent wave]] components. It is often preferred to the [[Sommerfeld identity]] when the field representation is needed to be in Cartesian coordinates.{{sfn|Chew|1990|p=65-75}} 

The resulting Weyl integral is commonly encountered in [[Monolithic microwave integrated circuit|microwave integrated circuit]] analysis and electromagnetic radiation over a stratified medium; as in the case for Sommerfeld integral, it is [[Numerical integration|numerically evaluated]].<ref name="chow-quick"/> As a result, it is used in calculation of Green's functions for [[Method of moments (electromagnetics)|method of moments]] for such geometries.{{sfn|Kinayman|Aksun|2005|p=268}} Other uses include the descriptions of [[electric dipole|dipolar]] emissions near surfaces in [[nanophotonics]],{{sfn|Novotny|Hecht|2012|p=335-338}}<ref name="weberford"/><ref name="abajo-light"/> [[holography|holographic]] [[inverse scattering problem]]s,<ref name="wolf-holography"/> Green's functions in [[quantum electrodynamics]]<ref name="agarwal-qm"/> and [[acoustic wave|acoustic]] or [[seismic wave]]s.{{sfn|Aki|Richards|2002|p=189-192}}
